561.title: Shurpanakha
561.hook: a visitor walks up to the hut at Panchavati and, within a minute, proposes marriage
561.carry: a joke can turn ugly fast
561.howItsDone: The Shurpanakha episode is a turning point in the Ramayana, and some modern writers, performers and commentators have revisited it from her side of the story.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Panchavati, part two. On a cold dawn walk, Rama stopped Lakshmana from blaming Kaikeyi: speak only of Bharata, he said. Did you steer a conversation toward praise? Day five hundred sixty-one.

The quiet ends the way a lot of trouble starts: with someone noticing someone. Rama is sitting outside the hut, talking with Sita and Lakshmana, when a rakshasi, a woman of the rakshasa people, comes through the trees and sees him. She stops. And she wants him, right then, completely. She walks straight up and asks: who are you, dressed like a hermit but carrying a bow, with a wife beside you, in a forest that belongs to rakshasas?
screen: `SOMEONE NOTICES SOMEONE.` → `A RAKSHASI AT THE HUT.` → `WHO ARE YOU, WITH A BOW?`

segments.voice: Rama answers her plainly. He tells her his name, his father's, Sita's and Lakshmana's, and why they're in the forest. Then he asks who she is. Her answer reshapes the whole story. I am Shurpanakha, she says, sister of Ravana, king of the rakshasas, and of Kumbhakarna, Vibhishana, and of Khara and Dushana, who rule this part of the forest. I saw you and I want you. Be my husband. Leave this woman. And then it turns ugly: she says she'll eat Sita, and Lakshmana too. Her name tells you how Valmiki sees her. Shurpa is a winnowing basket, the wide flat tray for sifting grain. Nakha is a fingernail. So, she of the nails like winnowing fans. Valmiki describes her as everything Rama isn't, line by line. Rama's response is to laugh, and to joke. He tells her he's married, and suggests she try his brother instead. Lakshmana jokes back: I'm only Rama's servant, you'd be a servant's wife. Go back to him. She goes back and forth between them, getting angrier. Here, honesty matters. Some readers have been uneasy with this scene: two princes teasing a woman whose feelings, however fierce, are real to her. Others read the teasing as a way of turning aside a dangerous situation without violence. The text doesn't stop to settle it. It hurries on. Because her anger is about to turn into something much worse.
screen: `SISTER OF RAVANA.` · `BE MY HUSBAND. LEAVE HER.` · `NAILS LIKE WINNOWING FANS.` · `THE BROTHERS JOKE.` · then, large: `SOME READERS ARE UNEASY.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle into your breath. Think of a time someone laughed at you, or a time you laughed at someone, when it wasn't really funny to the other person. Just notice it. No need to judge yourself or them. Feel where it lands in your body. Then breathe out slowly, and let your face soften, the jaw, the eyes, the mouth. Rest in that softness. The bell holds the time.
Shurpanakha. Ravana's sister, she of the nails like winnowing fans, who sees Rama and demands he marry her.
Your line: a joke can turn ugly fast. Today, before you joke at someone's expense, ask whether they'd laugh too. Day five hundred sixty-one.

562.title: Shurpanakha
562.hook: the joking stops when she lunges at Sita, and what follows will start a war
562.howItsDone: The mutilation of Shurpanakha is staged in Ramlila performances, and it is much discussed in modern Ramayana retellings and criticism.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shurpanakha, part one. Ravana's sister demanded Rama marry her, and the brothers answered with jokes: a joke can turn ugly fast. Did you check whether a joke would land kindly? Day five hundred sixty-two.

Shurpanakha has been sent back and forth between the brothers, laughed at, and refused. Now she turns on the person she blames. It's because of her, she says, looking at Sita. I'll eat her right now, and then you'll be mine. And she rushes at Sita. Valmiki compares it to a great meteor hurtling toward a gentle star. Sita, who has said nothing through any of this, is terrified. There's no more time for jokes.
screen: `SHE BLAMES SITA.` → `A METEOR AT A GENTLE STAR.` → `NO MORE JOKES.`

segments.voice: Rama catches her, holds her back, and speaks sharply to Lakshmana. We shouldn't joke with the cruel, he says. Look how close Sita came. Mark her, so she can't do this again. And Lakshmana draws his sword and cuts off her nose and ears. Shurpanakha flees screaming into the forest, bleeding, to her brother Khara at Janasthana. It's a violent scene, and a hard one to sit with. How have people read it? Some devotional readers see it simply: a rakshasi tried to kill Sita, and the brothers stopped her without taking her life. Others, especially modern readers, have found the punishment harsh, all the more after the teasing that came before. Different tellings handle it differently. In some later versions, like Kamban's Tamil Ramayana and Tulsidas's Hindi Ramcharitmanas, she first appears in a beautiful disguise, which changes how the scene feels. And in recent decades, writers have retold the story from Shurpanakha's own side: rejected, mocked, wounded. There's no single reading everyone shares, and it's fine to hold the discomfort. What the text makes plain is that this is a hinge in the story. Her wound goes first to Khara, and from Khara, the story will travel to Lanka, to Ravana. A rejected proposal at a hut by a river leads, step by step, to Sita's abduction and a war. Valmiki lets you watch it happen: a disaster that starts small, with hurt and pride on more than one side.

Just breathe with the knowledge that small moments matter, and let your breath stay calm and even. The bell holds the time.
Shurpanakha. She attacks Sita, Lakshmana cuts off her nose and ears, and she flees to Khara. The road to war begins here.
Your line: a disaster that starts small. Today, notice one small moment of hurt or pride before it grows, yours or someone else's. Day five hundred sixty-two.

563.title: Khara and Dushana
563.hook: a wounded sister reaches her brother's court, and an army of fourteen thousand gets ready to march
563.howItsDone: Valmiki lingers over the omens before the battle at Janasthana, and Rama's choice to send Sita and Lakshmana to safety is a familiar scene in performances.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shurpanakha, part two. She lunged at Sita, Lakshmana cut off her nose and ears, and she fled to Khara: a disaster that starts small. Did you notice a small hurt before it grew? Day five hundred sixty-three.

Shurpanakha falls at her brother's feet, covered in blood. Khara rules Janasthana, the rakshasa stronghold in Dandaka, with his general Dushana. He's furious, and he's proud, and both show. Who did this to you? Tell me and I'll drink their blood. She tells him: two young men in bark clothes, with bows, and a woman. Khara's first move is almost casual. He sends fourteen rakshasas to kill them, and to bring their blood back for his sister.
screen: `AT KHARA'S FEET.` → `WHO DID THIS?` → `FOURTEEN SENT TO KILL.`

segments.voice: The fourteen arrive at Panchavati with Shurpanakha pointing the way. Rama asks Lakshmana to stay by Sita, then speaks to the rakshasas first. We live here as hermits, he says, at the sages' request. If you've come to fight, stop where you are. They don't stop. They hurl their spears, and Rama's arrows cut down all fourteen. Shurpanakha runs back to Khara screaming, and this time she shames him. You call yourself a warrior and you sent fourteen? Now Khara is truly enraged. He calls up his whole force: fourteen thousand rakshasas, with Dushana and with Trishiras, the three-headed. As they march, the omens turn against them. Valmiki piles them up: a rain of blood, jackals howling, the sun dimmed, Khara's left arm throbbing. Khara ignores every one. Back at the hut, Rama sees signs too, and reads them. Then he does something unexpected. He tells Lakshmana to take Sita to a cave in the mountain, hidden by trees, and stay with her there. I'll face them alone, he says. Lakshmana could argue. He doesn't. He takes his bow and Sita and goes. That's the shape of today: a small attack, a humiliation, an overwhelming answer, and a man who decides to stand in front of it by himself, so that the people he loves are out of reach.
screen: `FOURTEEN AT PANCHAVATI.` · `SHE SHAMES KHARA.` · `FOURTEEN THOUSAND MARCH.` · `TAKE SITA TO THE CAVE.` · then, large: `I'LL FACE THEM ALONE.`

segments.voice: Sit steady, as if you're standing your ground. Feel your seat solid underneath you, your spine long. Think of one person you'd want to keep out of harm's way. Khara. Harsh by name, the rakshasa lord of Janasthana, who sends fourteen, then fourteen thousand, against Rama, with his general Dushana.
Your line: I'll face them alone. Today, take on one hard thing yourself so someone you love doesn't have to. Day five hundred sixty-three.

564.title: Khara and Dushana
564.hook: the sages and the gods gather in the sky to watch one man stand in front of an army
564.howItsDone: The battle of Janasthana is told in many Ramlila performances, and devotees often point to it as the moment Rama's promise to the forest sages is fulfilled.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Khara and Dushana, part one. Fourteen thousand marched, and Rama sent Sita and Lakshmana to a cave: I'll face them alone, he said. Did you take on a hard thing for someone? Day five hundred sixty-four.

Rama puts on his armor, strings his bow, and waits outside the empty hut. Valmiki says the sages, the gods and the celestial beings gather in the sky above Janasthana to watch. Some of them are worried. One man against fourteen thousand. They pray for him aloud. Then the dust rises on the horizon, the drums get louder, and the army of Khara comes into view, a dark mass like storm clouds rolling in.
screen: `ARMOR ON, BOW STRUNG.` → `THE GODS WATCH FROM THE SKY.` → `AN ARMY LIKE STORM CLOUDS.`

segments.voice: The battle fills several chapters, and Valmiki tells it in detail. Rama's arrows fly so fast, he says, that the rakshasas can't see him draw or release, only the bow bending into a circle. The army falls back, regroups, and charges again. Dushana leads one assault and falls. Trishiras, the three-headed, comes next, and falls too. Then only Khara is left, and the fight between the two of them is fierce. Khara cuts Rama's bow, shatters his armor. Rama takes up another bow and goes on. Khara even tears up a tree and hurls it. Before the end, the two exchange taunts, and Rama names what Khara has done: the sages he has terrorized, the hermits killed in the forest. Finally Rama fits an arrow and Khara falls. The text says it was all over in a muhurta and a half, a little over an hour. The gods rain flowers. The sages come down and praise him. Then Lakshmana comes out of the cave with Sita, and Sita, seeing Rama alive, unhurt, surrounded by grateful sages, runs and holds him. A few days ago, Rama promised the sages to protect them. Sita asked whether that promise was wise. Today the promise is kept, at full cost, by one person. But one rakshasa, Valmiki says, slipped away from the field. His name is Akampana. And he's heading south, toward the sea, toward Lanka.
screen: `THE BOW BENT INTO A CIRCLE.` · `DUSHANA FALLS, THEN TRISHIRAS.` · `KHARA AND RAMA, ALONE.` · `SITA RUNS TO HIM.` · then, large: `ONE ESCAPES TO LANKA.`

565.title: Ravana and Maricha's warning
565.hook: the king of Lanka hears the news, makes a plan, and is talked out of it on the first try
565.carry: pride stung in public is harder to talk down
565.tomorrow: Ravana and Maricha's warning, part two
565.howItsDone: Recitations of the Aranya Kanda that tell this part in full keep Maricha's first refusal, so listeners hear that Ravana was talked out of the plan once before Shurpanakha's scolding changed his mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Khara and Dushana, part two. Rama alone defeated their army and kept his promise, but Akampana escaped toward Lanka: one escapes to Lanka. Did you keep a hard promise? Day five hundred sixty-five.

Until now, the Ramayana has spoken of Ravana without showing him. Now the story crosses the sea, into his city. Akampana arrives in Lanka shaking, and tells the king of the rakshasas everything: Janasthana is empty, Khara and Dushana are dead, fourteen thousand lie on the field, and one man did it. Ravana's first response is rage. Who is this man? I'll burn him. And Akampana says: you can't beat him. But I know how you can hurt him.
screen: `ACROSS THE SEA, IN LANKA.` → `ONE MAN DID THIS.` → `I KNOW HOW TO HURT HIM.`

segments.voice: Akampana's idea is cold. Rama has a wife, Sita, and no woman in the world, he says, is her equal in beauty. Carry her off, and Rama will die of grief without a single arrow. Ravana likes it. He takes his chariot across the sea to the hermitage of an old acquaintance, Maricha. Remember that name. Maricha is the rakshasa Rama spared years ago, at Vishvamitra's sacrifice, hurling him out to sea alive. He's lived as a kind of hermit since. Ravana tells him the plan and asks for help. And Maricha says no. Who told you to do this, he asks. Whoever it was is your enemy pretending to be your friend. Rama is a sleeping lion. Don't go poke him. Go home, enjoy your wives, and let him live with his. And here's the surprise. Ravana listens. He turns around and goes home to Lanka. If the story stopped there, it would be a story about good advice taken. But someone else is on her way to Lanka. Shurpanakha arrives at Ravana's court, mutilated, and she doesn't plead. She scolds. What kind of king are you, she says, lost in pleasure while a man destroys your army and your frontier? You don't even know what's happening in your own lands. And then she describes Sita, at length. The warning that worked once is about to be overruled. Pride, stung in public, is harder to talk down.

Let your breath slow, and rest in the first one. The bell holds the time.

Your line: pride stung in public is harder to talk down. Today, if your pride gets stung, wait an hour before you decide anything. Day five hundred sixty-five.

566.title: Ravana and Maricha's warning
566.hook: flatterers are everywhere, says an old rakshasa to his king; the person who tells you the hard truth is rare
566.carry: pleasant things are easy to find
566.tomorrow: Ravana and Maricha's warning, part three
566.howItsDone: Maricha's line ramo vigrahavan dharmah, Rama is dharma in bodily form, is quoted on its own in Hindu teaching, as are his lines on rare, honest advice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ravana and Maricha's warning, part one. Maricha talked Ravana out of the plan, until Shurpanakha shamed him in his court: pride stung in public is harder to talk down. Did you wait before deciding with stung pride? Day five hundred sixty-six.

Ravana sets out again in his flying chariot, along the coast. Valmiki slows down to paint it: the shore lined with coconut palms and sandalwood, pearls drying on the beaches, hermitages of sages, and the ships of merchants. Then the chariot lands at Maricha's hermitage for the second time. The old rakshasa, in bark clothes and matted hair, welcomes his king with food and water, and then asks, carefully: why have you come back?
screen: `A FLYING CHARIOT ALONG THE COAST.` → `PEARLS ON THE BEACHES.` → `WHY HAVE YOU COME BACK?`

segments.voice: Ravana spells out the plan. Turn yourself into a golden deer, spotted with silver, and wander near Rama's hut. Sita will want you. Rama and Lakshmana will go after you. Then I'll take her. Maricha begins with a saying: people who say pleasant things are always easy to find, king. But someone who says what is unpleasant and good for you, and someone who will listen to it, those are rare. Then he tells Ravana the truth he doesn't want. You don't know who Rama is. He wasn't sent to the forest for any crime. He went to keep his father's word. And then a short line in Sanskrit, ramo vigrahavan dharmah: Rama is dharma in bodily form. Right living, duty, truth, with a body and a bow. To steal his wife, Maricha says, is to walk into a fire. You'll ruin yourself, your city and your people. Notice who's speaking. Not a sage, not a god, not one of Rama's friends. A rakshasa, Rama's old enemy, who was once hurled across the sea by him. That's what gives the words their weight. He has met Rama as an enemy, and he speaks from that. And he's using everything he knows to try to save his own king from himself.

Breathe steadily. The bell holds the time.

567.howItsDone: Some Ramayana teachers use Maricha's confession, seeing Rama in every tree, as a striking example of how the mind dwells on what it fears, and some devotional readers see a strange kind of devotion in it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ravana and Maricha's warning, part two. Maricha told his king the hard truth: pleasant things are easy to find, and Rama is dharma in bodily form. Did you listen to something you'd rather not hear? Today the week closes. Day five hundred sixty-seven.

Maricha has given his king the argument. Now he gives him something more personal: his fear. Let me tell you how I know Rama, he says. I was strong once, and proud. I went to break up Vishvamitra's sacrifice, and a boy, barely grown, shot me with one arrow and threw me a hundred yojanas into the sea. I lived. And I didn't learn, not then. It took a second meeting to teach me.
screen: `NOT AN ARGUMENT: A FEAR.` → `A BOY WITH ONE ARROW.` → `INTO THE SEA, ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Later, Maricha says, I came into Dandaka with two others, all three of us in the shape of deer, eating sages. Rama saw us. He shot three arrows. My two companions died. I ran. Since then, he tells Ravana, I've given up all that. I live as a hermit. But I can't get away from him. I see Rama in every tree, dressed in bark, holding his bow. I see him in my dreams. Even words that start with his sound, ratna, jewel, ratha, chariot, frighten me. It's an astonishing confession for a villain to make, and it's very human. Then Ravana answers, and you can hear how the conversation was always going to end. I didn't come for advice, Ravana says. A king's minister speaks when asked. Do as I say, or I'll kill you now. Maricha sees the trap clearly. If I go, Rama kills me. If I refuse, you kill me. So he chooses. Better to die at the hands of an enemy like Rama, he says, than by my own king. And he goes. Now the week. Shurpanakha at the hut, and the brothers' jokes. The attack on Sita, and the wound that started the war. Fourteen, then fourteen thousand, and Rama standing alone. Akampana's escape. Ravana's first visit to Maricha, talked out of it, and then shamed into it. And Maricha's warning, the rarest kind of advice, refused.
screen: `THREE DEER, THREE ARROWS.` · `I SEE RAMA IN EVERY TREE.` · `OBEY, OR I KILL YOU NOW.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `BETTER TO DIE BY RAMA'S HAND.`

segments.voice: Sit and let your breath settle. Think of a fear that follows you around, something you keep seeing everywhere, the way Maricha saw Rama in every tree. Don't push it away, and don't feed it. Just name it softly. Then notice: right now, in this room, in this breath, is it actually here? Let your attention come back to the breath, the seat, the sounds. The bell holds the time.
Maricha, the rakshasa who confesses his fear, is threatened by Ravana, and agrees to go: better to die by Rama's hand than by his own king.
Your line: better to die by Rama's hand. Today, when you're the one in charge, ask for honest advice and let it change your mind. Day five hundred sixty-seven.

screen: `DAY 567 COUNTS.` → `A WEEK FROM PANCHAVATI TO LANKA, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: THE GOLDEN DEER.`

original.note: Sanskrit mārīca: the rakshasa spared at Siddhashrama, who becomes the golden deer.

trapdoor: what you thought: Maricha is a willing villain.
what it means: he warns, confesses his fear, and goes only under threat of death.
what a scholar hears: Aranya 38–41 hold his two memories of Rama, the 'ra' words that scare him, Ravana's threat, and his choice.
